# zufft

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufft/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufft/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zufft/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufft/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

zufft computes fast Fourier, cosine and sine transforms in R. It bundles the
BSD-licensed FFT code of [ducc0](https://github.com/mreineck/ducc), the same
files and commit that SciPy uses, so it needs no system FFTW library and
carries no GPL code.

- **Replaces fftwtools without FFTW.** `install.packages()` is enough, on
  every platform, and the licence is MIT.
- **Fast.** With CRAN's build, faster than fftwtools on 30 of 33 benchmark
  cases and within 1.26 times on the rest; threads help further.
- **Familiar.** Names a fftwtools user knows (`fft_c2c()`, `fft_r2c()`,
  `fft_c2r()`), the conventions of `scipy.fft` for axes, normalisation and
  cosine and sine transforms, and drop-in replacements for `stats::fft()`
  and `stats::mvfft()`.

## Installation

Install zufft from CRAN with:

``` r
install.packages("zufft")
```

or the development version from [GitHub](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufft)
with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")
```

## Example

```{r}
library(zufft)

x <- c(1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7)
fft_c2c(x)                       # full complex spectrum, as stats::fft(x)
X <- fft_r2c(x)                  # the non-redundant half
fft_c2r(X, n = length(x))        # and back

# columns of a matrix, on two threads
m <- matrix(rnorm(4096 * 64), 4096)
spec <- fft_r2c(m, axes = 1, workers = 2)
dim(spec)

# cosine and sine transforms, SciPy's definitions
fft_dct(x, norm = "ortho")
fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE)

# fast lengths for zero-padding
fft_next_len(1009)
```

## Coming from fftwtools or scipy.fft

`vignette("migrating-from-fftwtools")` maps every fftwtools function to
zufft. The one thing to remember is that zufft scales inverses by `1/n`, as
SciPy does; add `norm = "none"` for fftwtools' (and `stats::fft()`'s)
unscaled numbers. The
[scipy.fft article](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zufft/articles/zufft-for-scipy-users.html)
covers the Python side: the definitions match, and the test suite checks
2040 cases against SciPy.

## Speed

zufft does not need a native build to keep up with fftwtools. On a Linux
x86-64 runner, against fftwtools on Ubuntu's FFTW (built with SSE2 and AVX
vector code), one thread, from `bench/RESULTS.md`:

| Case | fftwtools | zufft, CRAN build | ratio | zufft native, ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1-D complex 1 048 576 | 27.02 ms | 20.64 ms | 0.76 | 0.59 |
| 1-D real 1 000 000 | 16.50 ms | 11.77 ms | 0.71 | 0.57 |
| columns real 1024 × 1024 | 5.97 ms | 2.55 ms | 0.43 | 0.34 |
| 2-D complex 2048² | 279.85 ms | 67.76 ms | 0.24 | 0.19 |
| 3-D complex 128³ | 44.80 ms | 34.10 ms | 0.76 | 0.83 |
| 1-D complex 100 000 | 1.44 ms | 1.81 ms | 1.26 | 0.83 |

A ratio below 1 means zufft is faster. With CRAN's portable build (SSE2),
zufft is faster on 30 of the 33 benchmark cases. The three where it is
slower are single 1-D complex transforms of about 10^5 to 10^6 points that
cannot be split into lines (worst 1.26 times). Built for the local CPU
(below, AVX2 here), zufft is faster on all 33. Each ratio compares runs on
the same machine; the two builds ran on separate runners.

Most of the margin comes from planning: zufft caches its plans, while
fftwtools builds a new FFTW plan on every call. Threads add more
(`workers = 2`), which fftwtools does not offer. Transforms of any length
run in O(n log n): a prime length of 100 003 takes milliseconds, against
seconds for `stats::fft()`.

On Apple silicon the gap is wider, but partly because Homebrew's FFTW has
no vector code for double precision there; `bench/RESULTS.md` has those
numbers too.

R stores arrays column by column, so the first dimension is the contiguous
one. With `axes = NULL` the real transforms halve that dimension, which is
fast and matches fftwtools; give `axes` explicitly to halve the last one
listed, as SciPy does. Results are bit-identical whatever the number of
threads.

**A native build** is the user's choice: CRAN's binaries use the portable
SSE2 (x86-64) or NEON (arm64) vector width. To compile for your own CPU, add
this line to `~/.R/Makevars` and reinstall from source:

```make
CXX17FLAGS += -march=native
```

`zufft_info()$simd_width` then reports the width you got. On the Linux
x86-64 runner of `bench/RESULTS.md`, where this gives AVX2, the
16384 × 64 complex column case drops from 15.39 ms to 9.17 ms and a
complex prime length of 10 007 from 659.6 µs to 389.5 µs.

## Licence

zufft is MIT-licensed. Its bundled ducc0 files are the "BSD-3-Clause OR
GPL-2.0-or-later" subset that SciPy vendors, used under BSD-3-Clause;
`inst/COPYRIGHTS` lists every copyright holder. No GPL-only ducc0 code is
included.
